questions.q: A probability space is formally the triple (Ω, F, P). What does F represent?
options: The set of every possible outcome
The sigma-algebra of events that P is defined on
The expected value of the random variable
The variance of the sample space
questions.explain: Ω is the sample space and P is the probability measure. F is the sigma-algebra: the collection of events that are actually allowed to be assigned a probability.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Kolmogorov's three axioms?
options: For disjoint events, the probability of their union is the sum of their probabilities
P(A) must equal P(Aᶜ) for every event A
questions.explain: The three axioms are non-negativity, total probability one, and countable additivity over disjoint events. P(A) = P(Aᶜ) is not a rule — in fact it only holds when P(A) = 0.5.

questions.q: Formally, what makes a function X: Ω → ℝ a random variable?
options: It must take only positive values
It must be measurable, so {ω : X(ω) ≤ x} is an event in F for every real x
It must have a finite sample space
questions.explain: The defining technical requirement is measurability: every set of the form {X ≤ x} must be an event we're allowed to assign a probability to, which is what makes P(X ≤ x) well-defined.

questions.q: If X ~ N(0, 1) (the standard normal distribution), what is P(X ≤ 0)?
questions.explain: The standard normal density is symmetric about 0, so exactly half the probability mass lies at or below 0: P(X ≤ 0) = F(0) = 0.5.

questions.q: For a continuous random variable X with density f(x), what is P(X = 3.0) for any specific value such as 3.0?
options: It equals the CDF at 3.0, F(3.0)
0, because only intervals carry probability for continuous random variables
questions.explain: For continuous random variables, probability is only assigned to intervals via the integral of the density; any single point has probability exactly 0, even though the density f(3.0) itself can be positive.
